questions.q: In the sentence "fe;k¡ ulh#íhu us vk¡[kksa osQ oaQps ge ij isQj fn,A" (page 22), the word 'oaQps' is not in the glossary. Using context clues from the surrounding dialogue, explain what 'oaQps' likely means and why the author chose this specific word instead of a simpler synonym like 'nkM+s'.
questions.a: 'OaQps' means 'fiercely/sharply/intensely'—describing how Fele Uljhan fixed her gaze on the narrator. The author chose it over 'nkM+s' because 'oaQps' carries a connotation of penetrating scrutiny mixed with suppressed emotion, matching Fele's character as someone who 'sees through' hypocrisy. A wrong answer treating it as merely 'angrily' misses the layered characterization Fele embodies throughout the story.

questions.q: The glossary defines 'v[kckjuohl' as 'i=kdkj' (editorial). On page 24, the character says: "ge rks v[kckj cukusokys vkSj v[kckj i<+usokys nksukas dks gh fuBYyk le>rs gSa". Explain why the author uses the abstract noun 'v[kckjuohl' (editorial-ship/editorial nature) here instead of the concrete 'v[kckj' (editorial), and how this grammatical shift reinforces the theme.
questions.a: The suffix '-ohl' (tatsam abstract noun marker) transforms the concrete task into a professional identity/ethos. The speaker asserts that both makers and readers of editorials share a *professional conscience*—not just a mechanical activity. A student who only translates it as 'editorial work' misses the thematic claim about journalistic integrity that drives the narrator's conflict with Fele.

questions.q: Compare the usage of 'rkyhe' in two sentences from page 24: (1) "rkyhe dh rkyhe gh cM+h ph”k gksrh gS" and (2) "rkyhe 'kCn dk nks ckj iz;ksx D;ksa fd;k gS". Analyze how repetition and syntactic position alter the semantic focus from 'small/little' to 'trivial/insignificant' in the first instance.
questions.a: In (1), the reduplication 'rkyhe dh rkyhe' (the very smallest of the small) + 'gh' (emphatic particle) + 'cM+h ph”k' (big mistake) creates an oxymoronic structure: the *tiniest* thing becomes the *biggest* error. The syntactic framing forces 'rkyhe' to mean 'seemingly trivial but actually consequential'. In (2), it's a meta-linguistic reference to the word itself. Missing this shift leads to flat translations like 'small mistake' in board answers.

questions.q: Evaluate the glossary definition of 'ulhgr' as 'lh[k] f'k{kk' (learning/education). Fele says on page 25: "dke djus ls vkrk gS] ulhgrksa ls ugha". Argue whether 'ulhgr' here means 'formal education' or 'bookish knowledge detached from practice', using at least two other scenes from the story as evidence.
questions.a: It means 'bookish knowledge detached from practice'. Evidence: (1) Fele mocks the narrator's inability to recognize a 'ckn'kkg lyker' despite his degrees (page 25). (2) She contrasts her practical skill ("jksVh idkus dk bYe") with his theoretical "bYe" (page 22). The glossary's 'f'k{kk' is the *dictionary* meaning; Fele weaponizes the *contextual* meaning to expose class prejudice. An answer citing only the glossary fails the 'analysis' requirement.

questions.q: Create an original 3-sentence mini-dialogue between two Class 11 students discussing a school event, correctly using *three* words from the chapter's glossary (e.g., 'eksgyr', 'yegk Hkj', 'ctk I+kQjekuk') in a way that preserves their contextual flavor from "fe;k¡ ulh#íhu".
questions.a: Student A: "Yaar, *eksgyr* nikal gaya taiyari ka, ab *yegk Hkj* se stage pe jaana padega." Student B: "Tension mat le, *ctk I+kQjekar* de dena—'Maine toh sirf duty nibhai hai, baaki sab aap logon ka pyaar hai.'" Poor answer uses them as mere synonyms for 'time', 'walk', 'speak well'.
